14-109.r: Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launch Station (TERLS) → set up in 1962 at Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala.

14-110.r: Sriharikota → barrier island in Andhra Pradesh that separates Pulicat Lake from the Bay of Bengal; home of India's satellite launch centre.

14-112.r: Kakrapar → nuclear power plant; Pokhran → atom bomb blast site; Thumba → rocket launching centre; Sriharikota → satellite launching station.

14-113.r: February 2004 blast → at a solid propellant plant of Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota.

14-114.r: Aeroplane wing: convex top, concave bottom → air flows faster over the top, so pressure is lower above, giving lift; R (slower air on top) is false.

14-115.r: 'Black Box' (flight data recorder + cockpit voice recorder) → painted heat-resistant bright orange so it is easy to find in crash wreckage.
14-115.t: Don't go by the name: the 'Black Box' is orange, not black.

14-116.r: The Moon → Earth's only natural satellite; the fifth largest satellite in our solar system.

14-117.r: Chandrayaan-1 (India's first Moon mission) → launched 22 October 2008 from Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh; entered lunar orbit 8 November 2008; worked till 29 August 2009.

14-120.r: Chandrayaan-2 → initially headed by Dr. M. Annadurai (also led Chandrayaan-1); later led by Muthayya Vanitha (Project Director) and Ritu Karidhal (Mission Director).

14-121.r: Chandrayaan-2 → approved 2008 under PM Manmohan Singh; lander Vikram, rover Pragyan; targeted the Moon's south polar region, NOT the north pole.

14-122.r: Chandrayaan-2 → launched 22 July 2019 from Sriharikota (Andhra Pradesh) by GSLV-MK III-M1; reached lunar orbit 20 August 2019.

14-123.r: Chandrayaan-2 launch vehicle → GSLV-MkIII-M1 (LVM3): three-stage heavy-lift rocket with cryogenic upper stage; 4 ton class to GTO or about 10 tons to LEO.

14-124.r: Chandrayaan-3 → follow-on to Chandrayaan-2 to show safe landing and roving; launched by LVM3; Vikram lander + Pragyan rover; India fourth country to soft-land on Moon.

14-126.r: APXS (Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer) on Chandrayaan-3's Pragyan rover → found elemental composition (Mg, Al, Si, K, Ca, Ti, Fe) of lunar soil; other payload: LIBS.

14-127.r: LUPEX (Chandrayaan-5) → India (ISRO)–Japan (JAXA) joint mission to the Moon's south pole, approved 10 March 2025; statement 2 on lander/rover roles is wrong.

14-128.r: Moon Express → world's first private flight plan to the Moon; approved by the Federal Aviation Administration on 3 August 2016.

14-129.r: China's Chang'e 6 → first to bring soil from the far (dark) side of the Moon; launched 3 May, landed 1 June, returned 25 June 2024.

14-130.r: Luna-25 (Roscosmos, August 2023) → failed lander near lunar south pole; first of China–Russia ILRS missions, rival to US-led Artemis Accord → A, R true, R explains A.

14-131.r: Aditya-L1 → ISRO's first space observatory to study the Sun, in halo orbit around Sun-Earth L1 (about 1.5 million km away); PSLV-C57, 2 September 2023.

14-132.r: Aditya-L1 → seven payloads: four view the Sun directly (VELC, SUIT, SoLEXS, HEL1OS); remaining three (ASPEX, PAPA, a magnetometer) study the L1 point.
14-132.h: Seven = four looking at the Sun + three sampling at L1.

14-133.r: Mangalyaan = Mars Orbiter Mission → launched 5 November 2013 by ISRO; in Mars orbit from 24 September 2014; India's first interplanetary mission.

14-135.r: Mangalyaan (MOM) → India first Asian nation and first in world to reach Mars orbit in first attempt; ISRO fourth agency (after USA, Soviet Union/Russia, EU), not second.

14-136.r: Axiom-4, SpaDeX and Gaganyaan → all three support microgravity research (near-weightless state in Low Earth Orbit).

14-137.r: China's Tiangong space station → final module launched: Mengtian; first (core) module: Tianhe, 29 April 2021.

14-138.r: Tianwen-1 → China's (CNSA) Mars spacecraft: orbiter, lander and Zhurong rover; launched 23 July 2020 on Long March 5.

14-139.r: Shenzhou-7 (China, 25 September 2008) → carried three astronauts, not four; Long March II-F rocket; first Chinese spacewalk; crew returned safely.

14-140.r: Micius (QUESS) → world's first quantum communications satellite, launched by China on 16 August 2016; named after an ancient Chinese philosopher.

14-141.r: NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) → joint NASA–ISRO Earth-observing radar satellite; partnership signed 2014; launch expected 2025.

14-142.r: CNES (Centre National d'Etudes Spatiales) → space agency of France; signed joint maritime surveillance agreement with ISRO in March 2019.

14-143.r: Arktika-M → Russia's satellite to monitor Arctic climate, launched 28 February 2021; can also relay distress signals (Cospas-Sarsat).

14-144.r: JAXA (Japan) → used steam (water propellant) to propel CubeSat EQUULEUS (November 2022), launched with Artemis 1; first such orbit control beyond low-Earth orbit.

14-145.r: World's smallest satellite-carrying rocket → launched by JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) in February 2018.

14-146.r: NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) → Pasadena, California, USA.

14-147.r: Greased Lightning-10 (GL-10) → NASA's battery-powered electric plane with 10 engines; takes off like a helicopter, flies like an aircraft.

14-148.r: SOFIA (Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy) → NASA mission that confirmed water molecules on the Moon's sunlit surface (Clavius Crater, October 2020).

14-149.r: Lunar Trailblazer (NASA, launched 26 February 2025) → to detect and map water on the Moon's surface; contact was lost and mission ended 31 July 2025.

14-150.r: Deep Impact (NASA, launched 12 January 2005) → crashed an impactor into comet Temple-1 (Tempel 1) nucleus on 4 July 2005, after 429 million km in 174 days.

14-151.r: Phoenix → NASA Mars Scout Program lander; landed on Mars 25 May 2008.

14-152.r: Spirit (MER-A) → first US rover to reach Mars, landed 4 January 2004 (active 2004–2010); twin rover Opportunity (MER-B).

14-153.r: NASA evidence for life on Mars → water (sulfates show past water), gypsum (a sulfate) and methane.

14-154.r: Massive underground lake (20 km across, 1.5 km beneath southern polar ice cap) → found on Mars; reported in journal 'Science', July 2018.

14-155.r: Methane in atmosphere → Mars (found by ESA's Mars Express, NASA's Curiosity) and Jupiter (traces; mainly hydrogen and helium); the book accepts both (c) and (d).

14-156.r: Saturn's atmosphere → about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium, with traces of methane, ammonia, water ice; among the options, methane fits best.

14-157.r: Least dense planet → Saturn (0.7 g/cm³); Earth densest (5.5), then Mercury (5.4), Venus (5.2), Mars (3.9).
